title: Is a Degree Still Worth It? A Break Room Debate
script: Sari: [pointed] I saw you reading another article about self-taught developers outearning graduates. You're building a case, aren't you?
Bimo: [amused] Maybe. I never finished my degree, and it still bothers me that people assume that means I cut corners somewhere.
Sari: [gentle] Nobody here thinks that, Bimo. You're one of the sharpest engineers on this floor.
Bimo: [candid] I appreciate that, but I still catch myself overcompensating in meetings, citing sources unnecessarily, as if I need to prove I did the reading nobody assigned me.
Sari: [thoughtful] That's a strange kind of pressure, proving competence you've already demonstrated a hundred times over.
Bimo: [reflective] It is. Though I'll admit there are gaps. Theoretical foundations I've had to backfill clumsily on my own, usually at midnight, usually under deadline pressure.
Sari: [honest] I had the opposite problem. Four years of theory and comparatively little practice, so my first year here felt like relearning the entire job from scratch.
Bimo: [curious] Do you think the degree was worth it, given that gap?
Sari: [measured] Mostly, yes, though not for reasons the university advertised. The actual value was learning how to sit with a hard, unresolved problem for months without abandoning it.
Bimo: [interested] That's not something you can easily fake your way into through tutorials alone.
Sari: [agreeing] Exactly, and I don't think self-teaching is inherently inferior, just differently shaped. You build resilience under deadline pressure that classroom learning rarely demands.
Bimo: [wry] We've essentially each spent years compensating for what the other one got for free.
Sari: [smiling] Which probably means the ideal path involves stealing shamelessly from both approaches rather than defending either one too rigidly.
Bimo: [conceding] Fair enough. I'll stop reading those articles as ammunition and start reading them as, I don't know, an actual map of what I'm missing.
